one_liner: Header-only radix/American-flag sort beating std::sort by ~2x on ints, floats, structs and strings via key extraction.
what_it_does: ska_sort is a single-header, non-comparison sort for random-access ranges. ska_sort(begin, end) sorts in place using the elements themselves as keys (default) or ska_sort(begin, end, extract_key) with a caller-supplied ExtractKey that returns an unsigned/radix-comparable value (integer, IEEE-754 float, bool, or a tuple/struct with operator[]). A separate ska_sort_copy(begin, end, buffer_begin[, key]) variant sorts into a caller-provided same-size buffer and returns a bool telling you whether the result ended up in the original range or the buffer.
how_it_is_fast: Recursively partitions elements byte-by-byte into 256 buckets (LSD-style radix sort) instead of comparing elements, giving roughly O(n*b) behavior for b key bytes versus std::sort's O(n log n). For partitions under the American-flag-sort threshold (1024 elements) it uses an in-place American flag sort whose inner loop ('ska byte sort') processes swaps for many not-yet-placed elements at once rather than completing one swap chain at a time, improving instruction-level parallelism. Partitions under 128 elements, or string keys whose recursion exceeds 16 levels (pathological shared prefixes), fall back to std::sort.
when_to_use: Large arrays (roughly >128 elements) of integers, IEEE-754 floats, bools, or other types with a cheap ExtractKey returning a radix-sortable value
Structs/tuples sorted by a fixed-width key (128-1024 byte records in the author's benchmarks), via an ExtractKey with operator[]
Skewed/low-entropy integer distributions, where the author reports the largest wins ('many times faster' on std::geometric_distribution(0.001))
Throughput-focused batch sorts where instability and an optional O(n) auxiliary buffer (ska_sort_copy) are acceptable
Header-only C++ codebases that want to vendor one file rather than add a build dependency
when_not_to_use: You need a stable sort — ska_sort is not stable
Keys aren't radix-extractable, or the container isn't random-access — this fails to compile rather than silently falling back to std::sort
Very large collections: one blog-comment reader reports ska_sort slower than std::sort on 1.2 billion uint64_t (unverified, possibly paging-related)
Long, variable-length strings with many shared prefixes — the author says it degrades toward O(n log n) behavior there
Strict C++20 builds: the header uses std::result_of (deprecated C++17, removed C++20), and the repo has been unmaintained since 2017 so this is unlikely to be patched upstream

integration.dependencies: none for ska_sort.hpp (STL only: <cstdint>, <algorithm>, <type_traits>, <tuple>, <utility>); the bundled ska_sort_tests_and_benchmarks.cpp additionally needs GTest and Google Benchmark to build, but that file is not required to use the sort
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (generic lambdas); std::result_of usage makes strict C++20 mode risky without patching
integration.platforms: any (plain C++, no SIMD/intrinsics); float/double keys assume IEEE-754 representation
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: ska_sort(begin, end) is a near drop-in in-place replacement for std::sort(begin, end) on random-access iterators, but non-identity keys need an ExtractKey returning a radix-sortable value (not an arbitrary comparator), and the faster ska_sort_copy path requires a caller-managed same-size buffer plus checking its bool return to know which buffer holds the sorted result

gotchas: ska_sort_copy's bool return says whether the sorted output landed in buffer_begin (true) or the original range (false); using the wrong one silently gives unsorted/stale data

Float/double keys are reinterpreted as unsigned integers through a union, which is undefined behavior in standard C++, with no compile-time IEEE-754 (is_iec559) guard — flagged in open issue #2, never fixed
Types without a usable ExtractKey/subscript operator fail to compile rather than falling back to std::sort

Open issue #3 (2017) reports MSVC/VS2015 'class template has already been defined' compile errors for some custom key types; the repo's last two commits addressed similar SFINAE issues but the issue was never closed
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ska_sort over pdqsort/vergesort when your keys are natively radix-extractable (fixed-width ints/floats, short strings, small structs) and you want a small single-header drop-in with no build dependency; pdqsort and vergesort are comparison sorts with broader type support and adaptivity to existing order, and Highway's vqsort needs AVX-512/SIMD hardware plus a real build dependency, both heavier asks than ska_sort's plain C++14 header.
verified_claims_summary: The only benchmark is the author's 2016 blog post (Google Benchmark, ns/item charts) reporting ska_sort about 2x faster than std::sort on uniform-distribution integers and 'many times faster' on skewed (std::geometric_distribution(0.001)) integers, with similar or better results for (bool,float) pairs, 128-1024 byte structs, and short strings; no compiler, flags, or CPU model are stated, and the post itself notes performance degrades toward std::sort's O(n log n) on long strings with shared prefixes.
status_note: Abandoned since the last commit on 2017-05-15 (5 open issues, no README, no LICENSE file though BSL-1.0 is stated in the file headers); it is a single copy-pasteable header, so age is low-risk to vendor, but expect to patch std::result_of yourself for a C++20 toolchain.
